ab_stanley_headwall.blurb: Stanley Headwall is a tall limestone face at the foot of Stanley Peak, reached from the Stanley Glacier trailhead off Highway 93 South. It began as an ice and mixed destination and still holds a handful of serious winter lines, but the rock side is now mostly technical, balancey sport climbing, with a few longer multipitch lines. Most of the sport climbs fall in the 5.12 range, with some 5.11 and a few 5.13s, and Clockwork Orange and Vielfrass are two of the better-known ones. The crag sits in a scree bowl with little wind protection and gets morning sun, so belays can be cool. A creek and waterfall run close by.
ab_stanley_headwall.parking_note: Use the Stanley Glacier trailhead lot on the south side of Highway 93 South, a little over eight miles from Castle Junction.
ab_stanley_headwall.approach: Start up the Stanley Glacier trail and climb its switchbacks, then leave it on the unmarked lower branch. Contour across scree toward the drainage under the main waterfall. The crag is roughly 50 m right of the falls, with cairns marking the final stretch.

ab_lower_tier_of_drywood.blurb: The lower tier of Drywood sits on the north side of Drywood Mountain in Castle Wildland, in the far southwest corner of Alberta. It is a sport crag best known for a huge, steep cave, one of the biggest in the province, where the climbing runs nearly horizontal for thirty to forty feet and demands a lot from the forearms. Most routes fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with a few 5.13s and a small number of easier lines. Fear of Commitment (5.11a) is the one that stands out. The walk in is long enough to plan for, and riding a bike along the road shortens it.
ab_lower_tier_of_drywood.approach: Expect about an hour of travel in total, mostly along the road. Riding a bike up the road cuts it to roughly ten minutes of pedaling plus a half-hour walk.

ab_industrial_playground.blurb: Industrial Playground is a sport sector on the east side of Tunnel Mountain, just above the town of Banff. The routes cover a grid-bolted slab, so the climbing rewards balance, footwork and patience on small holds more than raw power. Nearly everything falls in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, with a few 5.9s and one easier line, which makes it a good place to work on slab technique. Digitalized Chaos (5.10a) is the one to know. The crag is close to town and quick to reach, and it tends to see steady traffic.

ab_birdwatchers.blurb: Birdwatchers is a south-facing sandstone crag off Highway 68 in Kananaskis, an easy day trip from Calgary. Because it faces the sun, it is a suntrap, and on clear days it stays comfortable well into the cold months, with little seepage from melting snow. The routes are mostly sport with some trad, and the bulk fall between 5.9 and 5.11, with a few 5.12s. The cliff is split into several sectors, and the walk in is steep but short, up a built trail through trees to the left end of the wall.
ab_birdwatchers.parking_note: Take Highway 40 south about 8 km to the Highway 68 turnoff, then drive 4 km of gravel. A small pullout on the south side of the road is often muddy, so roadside space on the north side works better.
ab_birdwatchers.approach: Walk west along the road, spot a flagged pine, and cross the meadow to a wooden staircase beside a boulder. Switchback up through the trees to the left end of the cliff, about 1 km with 230 m of climbing.

ab_black_band.blurb: Black Band is a south-facing sport cliff on the back side of Tunnel Mountain, a short walk from Banff. It stays sunny and warm, so it is popular early in the spring when other crags are still damp. Most of the climbing is well-bolted sport up to about 30 m, concentrated in the 5.10 range, with a few easier lines, a handful of boulder problems and a couple of trad routes. Sunburn (5.10c) and Domino (5.10a) are the standouts. Blocks have come off the cliff in spring, so be mindful of the trail below and keep off the scree slope.
ab_black_band.approach: Take the steps down behind the lot and follow the Hoodoo trail to a bend in the Bow River. Bear left, then follow the climbers' path uphill beside the scree rather than crossing it.

ab_outhouse_wall.blurb: Outhouse Wall is the biggest cliff at Back of the Lake, the quartzite buttresses at the far end of Lake Louise. The climbing is steep to vertical and mostly sport, with a good number of trad routes too, and the grades run from easy up to the very hard, with the heart of it between 5.10 and 5.12. Public Enemy (5.10a), Wicked Gravity (5.11a) and Mardi Gras (5.11a) are popular picks. Belayers get a view back down the lake toward the Chateau. Many routes can still be climbed in light summer rain, though some feel slick when chalked.
ab_outhouse_wall.parking_note: Drive to Lake Louise and use the lot just short of the Chateau, then continue on foot along the shore.
ab_outhouse_wall.approach: Walk the lakeshore trail to its far end, where it climbs over a rise and drops again. Where it descends again beside the rock, head left and climb along the foot of the cliff to the wall.

ab_hemingway_wall.blurb: Hemingway Wall is a short limestone sport wall just inside Grotto Canyon, near Canmore in the Bow Valley. It sits on the left side of the canyon not far from Water Wall. Nearly all of it is sport, and the climbing is technical, with plenty of small edges, so footwork matters more than strength. Routes run from a few easy lines through the 5.12s and a few 5.13s, with the largest group at 5.12. The Importance of Being Earnest (5.12a/b), Death in the Afternoon (5.12a) and Farewell to Arms (5.11a) are the best known. The walk in is gentle, so it works for a short outing.
ab_hemingway_wall.parking_note: From Canmore, follow Bow Valley Trail past Gap Lake and the Baymag plant, then turn left into the Grotto Canyon lot.

ab_big_brother.blurb: Big Brother is one of three tall granite boulders set in a downtown Calgary park, part of an outdoor urban bouldering installation. The three blocks mix overhangs, slabs and technical faces, and Big Brother carries the most problems, from easy up to the double digits, with the thick of them between V4 and V7. Rhino Dyno (V3), Who Nose (V4) and The Motion (V1-2) are among the favorites. The boulders are tall enough that a rope is rigged on top for climbing back down, and the landing is wood chips, so bring a crash pad. It is busy after work and on weekends.

az_gate_s_pass.blurb: Gate's Pass is a bouldering area in the Tucson Mountains, a short drive west of downtown Tucson, among saguaros in classic Sonoran Desert setting. The rock is volcanic, with sharp edges, pockets and good friction, though some of it is loose. Problems run from V0 up to V10, with a lot of them in the V0 to V1 range and a notable cluster at V4, including The Humbler (V4 X) and Shelf traverse (V4). The boulders sit close to the road, so a day's worth is within easy reach. It is a winter spot, and the season is fairly short. Watch for jumping cholla and snakes.
az_gate_s_pass.parking_note: Drive west from downtown Tucson on Speedway over the pass and down the steep far side, then use the second pullout on either side of the road. It takes about 15 minutes.
az_gate_s_pass.approach: The boulders are visible from the road on the south side. Follow established trails uphill.

az_neptune.blurb: Neptune is a busy crag in the Reef of Rocks, in the upper stretch of the Catalina Highway on Mount Lemmon. It is mostly traditional climbing with a smaller group of sport lines, and routes range from easy to 5.14-, with the thick of it between 5.10 and 5.12. Rapture of the Steep (5.10), Red Tide (5.13a) and Maiden Voyage (5.12b) are the headline climbs. Locals treat the Reef as a place to climb in hot weather, when Tucson is baking, and it feels unpleasant when cold. Bring a full trad rack with small gear.
